story: It starts down low. The first things you see are socks hanging to dry and, behind them, a window at sidewalk level: legs passing by, a fumigation truck, the city happening at the height of your ceiling. The camera descends slowly and drops you into a basement where four people fold pizza boxes and chase the neighbor's wifi like someone hunting for signal on the open sea. You laugh. It matters that you laugh, because that laugh is the door in. Then you go up. A kid with a rock in his backpack and a fake paper in his pocket crosses a gate and walks into a house designed by someone who's never been in a hurry: clean concrete, a huge window like a cinema screen, a lawn so green it looks hand-ironed. And it works. One gets in, then another, and the plan unfolds with the elegance of a well-told card trick: quick editing, harpsichord music, the dirty euphoria of watching someone get away with it. That's where the film breathes. An empty house, a long table, someone else's whisky, the warm feeling of finally having arrived somewhere. You settle into that comfort almost as much as they do. And then it starts to rain. The story stops climbing and starts descending, step by step, street by street, to a point where comedy no longer knows how to help you. It closes on something nobody says out loud but everyone notices: a smell, which ends up deciding more than any contract.
context_bullets: 2019, the peak of the new Korean cinema (Bong Joon-ho).
Palme d'Or winner and the first non-English-language film to win Best Picture at the Oscars.
Expect a tone that shifts from comedy to thriller, biting and elegant.

before_watching.text: The Parks' mansion doesn't exist: it was built as an open-air set, and the upper floors were added with visual effects. Bong storyboarded the whole thing himself.
It won the Palme d'Or unanimously and became the first non-English-language film to win the Best Picture Oscar.
Bong calls himself 'a lover of staircases' and organizes the film along an up/down axis. It starts as comedy and shifts tone without warning: go in knowing nothing.

fun_facts.text: The semi-basement apartment and its street were built inside a giant water tank so they could be flooded; on the last day they poured in real sewage water.
'Ram-don' doesn't exist in any language: translator Darcy Paquet made it up to subtitle jjapaguri, fusing 'ramen' and 'udon.'
There's a black-and-white cut regraded shot by shot with the cinematographer, not a simple filter; it premiered at the Rotterdam Film Festival.
The little song about 'Jessica, only child, Illinois, Chicago' is sung to the tune of 'Dokdo Is Our Land,' a popular Korean song students use as a memorization trick.

author_voice.text: Bong defines his film as "a comedy without clowns, a tragedy without villains, that spills into a violent entanglement and a headfirst fall down the stairs." And he qualifies the point about the protagonists: "It's not that they were parasites from the start. They're our neighbors, friends, and coworkers, who've simply been pushed to the edge of the cliff."

On his formal obsession: "You could say I'm a lover of staircases." And on the meaning of the rich family's house: the garden "almost feels surreal" seen through the giant window that frames it "like a screen," with the tall trees functioning as "the line Mr. Park always talks about. Don't cross the line."

On why smell: "Normally in real life it's not easy for poor people to get that close to rich people: first class, economy class, always separate. In this film they're very close. They can even smell each other." And he adds: "Smell reflects your life. It shows whether you're struggling. What kind of work you do."

emotional_temperature: Starts as a con-artist comedy and twists in your hands: it changes tone without warning. Go in knowing nothing and let it drag you downhill.
why_now: In August 2022, several people drowned in their banjiha in Seoul during flooding, and the city announced it would stop issuing permits for semi-basement housing; the international press literally called them "Parasite-style apartments." Thirteen years of rising housing costs and unevenly distributed climate risk have turned a vertical metaphor into an urban-planning statistic. In 2025, a New York Times survey of more than 500 film professionals ranked it the best film of the 21st century: it didn't age, we caught up to it.

metaphors.text: Verticality as a caste system: no one explains the hierarchy because the geography already does. Bong openly calls it "staircase cinema" and admits to being "a lover of staircases"; the up/down axis works exactly like the social elevator sociologists talk about, except here it only goes down fast.

Smell as an unfakeable border: you can fake a degree, an accent, and a résumé, but not the air you carry on you. It's the sensory version of what Bourdieu called habitus, a form of symbolic capital that slips in through the nose. Bong states it without theory: "Smell reflects your life."

Jjapaguri topped with hanwoo sirloin: two packets of instant noodles (end-of-the-month food) crowned with one of the country's most expensive cuts of beef. It's a class Frankenstein dish, inequality served in a single bowl and stirred in a hurry.

The rain as an unfair distribution of risk: for some it's a lovely night and a wet lawn; for others it's the loss of everything they own. It works as an early definition of climate vulnerability, the idea that the same weather event produces inconveniences upstairs and catastrophes downstairs.

intertextual_refs.text: 'The Housemaid' (Kim Ki-young, 1960), the Korean matrix of the story: a well-off family destabilized by domestic help, with the staircase as the stage for conflict. Bong has said Kim Ki-young "is my mentor and I watch his films over and over."

'Psycho' (Hitchcock, 1960): Bong recalls that as a child he was more fascinated by the house behind the motel than the motel itself, especially the second floor and the detective's slow climb up the stairs.
'The Servant' (Joseph Losey, 1963) and Claude Chabrol's films — 'La Cérémonie,' 'Que la bête meure' — are among the films Bong revisited in preproduction.

The real-life case of the Papin sisters (France, 1933), two maids employed by the Lancelin family whose story Bong has cited when discussing the film: an event French philosophy and psychoanalysis turned into an emblem of domestic class violence.

production_trivia.text: Filming ran from May 18 to September 19, 2018, in Seoul and Jeonju, on a budget of about $11.4 million that ended up generating $258 million at the worldwide box office.
The Parks' house doesn't exist: it was built from scratch. The ground floor and garden were built outdoors on a backlot and the upper floors were added with visual effects in post-production.

The semi-basement apartment and its street are also a set, built inside a giant pool at the Goyang Aqua Studio precisely so they could be flooded. Bong: "Since we had to flood the whole neighborhood, we built it inside a giant pool, a water tank. And on the last day of shooting we poured in sewage water."

Bong storyboarded the film shot by shot and drew the storyboards himself, later published as a graphic novel ('Parasite: A Graphic Novel in Storyboards'). Cinematographer Hong Kyung-pyo worked from that material.
The personal origin: as a young man Bong worked as a private tutor in a wealthy family's home and described the feeling as "infiltrating the private life of complete strangers."

There's a black-and-white version, regraded shot by shot together with Hong Kyung-pyo (not a simple filter). It premiered at the Rotterdam Film Festival in January 2020 and later reached U.S. theaters through NEON.
It was shot on an Alexa 65 camera, which allowed for wide, immersive shots without resorting to super-wide-angle lenses, key to letting the house's spaces breathe and the semi-basement suffocate.
The famous jingle "Jessica, only child, Illinois, Chicago" is sung to the tune of "Dokdo Is Our Land," a popular 1982 Korean song students commonly use as a mnemonic trick to memorize facts.

scene_analysis.scene: The opening shot: socks, window, street
scene_analysis.text: The film begins looking upward from the semi-basement: socks hanging in the foreground, the window as a frame, and, in the background, the city's feet. The camera descends until it finds the first character's face, and that descent establishes the film's entire grammar in ten seconds. The vertical framing of the start — looking down at the poor from above — will reverse once the son begins to climb socially.

The garden is always seen through a huge pane of glass Bong describes as "a screen": the rich don't live in nature, they consume it framed. The tall trees in the background function, in the director's own words, as "the line" Mr. Park talks about, the one you shouldn't cross. It's a border drawn with landscaping instead of a wall.

The long downhill journey through the storm is the point where comedy stops protecting the viewer: the film abandons the plan's brisk editing and adopts a continuous, gravitational, almost documentary-like movement. That the neighborhood was built inside a water tank so it could actually be flooded is not a minor technical detail: the sequence depends on the water behaving like water, not like an effect.

critical_consensus.summary: A nearly unprecedented critical consensus: it was read as the perfect synthesis of popular and auteur cinema, able to move audiences from laughter to horror without changing register. Rotten Tomatoes sums it up: "An urgent and brilliantly layered look at timely social issues, Parasite finds writer-director Bong Joon Ho in near-total command of his craft." On Metacritic, the 56 reviews collected are 100% positive. Dissenting voices exist and are a minority: they point to implausibilities in the plot and to a political message that describes the problem without proposing anything. In June 2025, a New York Times survey of more than 500 industry professionals ranked it the best film of the 21st century.
awards: Palme d'Or at Cannes 2019: the first Korean film to win it and the jury's first unanimous decision since 2013
Oscar for Best Picture (92nd Academy Awards): the first non-English-language film to achieve it
Oscar for Best International Feature Film
Golden Globe for Best Foreign Language Film
BAFTA for Best Original Screenplay and Best Film Not in the English Language
SAG Award for Best Ensemble: the first international film to win it

strengths: Total control of tone: it moves from con-artist comedy to thriller to drama with no visible seams, and every genre shift is also a shift in the viewer's moral position.

Architecture as screenplay: the house, the staircase, and the window tell the story before the dialogue does, thanks to production design built from scratch and a storyboard drawn shot by shot by the director himself.
The ensemble cast, especially Song Kang-ho, able to hold a character's dignity while the film pulls the ground out from under him; the SAG Award for Best Ensemble recognized this explicitly.
weaknesses: The mechanics of the plan demand very generous credulity from the Parks and a string of fortunate coincidences; some critics flagged this as implausibility in service of the thesis, and some found it overlong besides.

Its politics are diagnostic rather than prescriptive: it describes the system with enormous precision but deliberately leaves the horizon empty, which has allowed opposite readings — from 'radical' to 'conservative' — and, for some, makes it a film that's comfortable to applaud from above.
verdict: It's the film that proved Korean-language genre cinema could be, at once, the year's most effective entertainment and the decade's best essay on inequality: the exact point where world cinema stopped having an English-language center.
questions: If the Kims had other real options, would you still judge their plan the same way?
Who exactly is the parasite of the title, and what does the answer that came to you first say about you?
Is there something about you — a way of speaking, a neighborhood, a smell — you couldn't disguise no matter how much money you made?
debate_prompts: Ki-taek kills Mr. Park not over months of prior humiliation, but over a simple grimace of disgust at a smell in the middle of the party. Is the murder the film's logical climax, or a tonal misstep that betrays its own comedic pulse?
cta: This time ignore the dialogue and watch just one thing: when the camera goes up and when it goes down. The whole film is that count, and once you start keeping it you can't stop.
useless_fact: The word "ram-don" doesn't exist in Korean, English, or any language: translator Darcy Paquet made it up to subtitle jjapaguri (a homemade mix of two Nongshim instant noodles, Jjapaghetti and Neoguri), fusing "ramen" and "udon" because it seemed like the only thing an international audience would recognize. He googled it before writing it down and nothing came up. A dish millions of people cooked in 2020 carried a name a translator pulled out of thin air: the film that asked the world to get over "the one-inch barrier of subtitles" traveled, literally, on a made-up word.
